title: Predictive Holonomy and Minimal Completion of Coarse Dynamics
abstract:
arXiv:2610.13951v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A coarse description of a dynamical system generally fails to evolve autonomously: evolving and coarse-graining in different orders gives different predictions, and the compressed propagator fails the semigroup law. We show that this path dependence is the observable boundary of missing state. For a finite continuous-time Markov chain with generator $L$, coarse channel $C$, and stochastic section $R$ satisfying $CR=I$, define $P=RC$, $Q=I-P$, and $K=CLR$. The exact coarse propagator $T_t=C\mathrm{e}^{tL}R$ obeys a Volterra equation with memory kernel $\mathcal{M}(t)=CLQ\,\mathrm{e}^{tQLQ}\,QLR$. Every memory jet $\mathcal{M}^{(k)}(0)$ is recursively recoverable from the short-time derivatives of $T_t$ alone. The rank of the block Hankel operator $\mathbb{H}_{\infty}=(\mathcal{M}^{(i+j)}(0))_{i,j\geq 0}$ is exactly the smallest number of auxiliary linear state variables required to turn the coarse dynamics into an exact autonomous, time-homogeneous system. A minimal completion is constructible by Ho--Kalman factorization and is unique up to similarity. If $d=\min\{k:\mathcal{M}^{(k)}(0)\neq 0\}$, then every smooth classical $f$-divergence generically scales as $t^{2d+4}$. Exact Markov examples realize exponents $4,6,8$ and closure ranks $1,2,3$. We also derive finite-sample singular-value certificates for hidden predictive coordinates, including a matrix-Bernstein bound with intrinsic-variance control. Finally, histories are identified when they induce the same future law under every admissible intervention, yielding the minimal counterfactual predictive state. The results turn coarse-graining into a constructive state-completion problem and separate ordinary linear realization from the harder requirement of a positive or Markov realization.

title: Detector-Frame Quantum Limits for Heterodyne Timing in Relativistic Optical Links
authors: Salman Sajad Wani, Aatif Kaisar Khan, Saif Al-Kuwari, Mir Faizal
abstract:
arXiv:2610.13963v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-baseline optical links for space interferometry and satellite quantum networks rely on heterodyne phase tracking under Doppler motion and gravitational frequency shifts. These relativistic shifts can generate large detector-frame beat-frequency offsets over finite readout windows and thereby constrain the temporal precision of front-end phase readout. We develop a detector-frame framework for this problem using an effective two-mode signal--local-oscillator model in which relativistic motion rescales the local-oscillator frequency. Within this setting we derive closed-form Mandelstam--Tamm and Margolus--Levitin bounds for representative Gaussian resources and connect global state distinguishability with the operational precision of heterodyne phase tracking. In the bright-local-oscillator regime we identify a geometric--operational mismatch: the joint optical state can evolve on arbitrarily short global timescales while the relevant information rate is set by the measured detector record. Combining this result with an open-loop transient-acquisition analysis, we show that white phase noise and relativistic beat-frequency drift that is approximately constant over the acquisition window generate a cube-root scaling benchmark for the optimal pre-lock open-loop integration window and the minimum residual phase error. These results establish detector-frame benchmarks for quantum-limited heterodyne timing in relativistic optical links and clarify how global dynamical bounds enter task-restricted continuous optical measurements.

title: Comment on arXiv:2510.21705 "Fundamental Impossibility of a Superradiant Neutrino Laser" and comment on arXiv:2510.21692 "Can Bose-Einstein Condensates Enhance Radioactive Decay?"
abstract:
arXiv:2610.13967v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We show that the small value of the neutrino cross-section rules out superradiance in the laboratory.

title: Empirical Scaling Laws of Quantum Vision Transformers
authors: Yuqing Li, Fengyi Gao, Xin Jin, Xiaowei Jia, Qi Cheng, Junyu Liu
abstract:
arXiv:2610.13970v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum machine learning (QML) is a promising application of quantum computing, yet when and how practical learning models can achieve quantum advantage remains poorly understood. Even a polynomial improvement in the resources needed to attain a given predictive performance would be significant. In this work, we investigate empirical scaling laws of quantum vision transformers (QViTs), which connect QML to the transformer architecture underlying modern large language models. We ask whether QViTs exhibit scaling behavior analogous to classical models and how this behavior changes when qubit number is included alongside dataset size and model parameters. The validation losses in our numerical image-classification experiments are well described by a joint shifted power-law model in qubit number, transformer depth, and training dataset size. Expressing this fit in terms of the classical encoder parameter budget identifies a regime in which increasing the number of qubits can compensate for fewer classical encoder parameters at comparable predicted performance. This finding is consistent with earlier observations of parameter efficiency in quantum learning models and suggests a direction for exploring possible resource savings in QML.

title: Parameter-Efficient Multilinear Readout for Quantum Reservoir Computing
abstract:
arXiv:2610.13974v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) uses fixed quantum dynamics as a high-dimensional feature map. Still, standard pipelines flatten reservoir measurements and train a linear readout, ignoring the natural tensor structure across time steps, qubits, and observables. We propose a multilinear readout for quantum reservoir computing (ML-QRC), a tensor-structured neural readout compressed through mode-wise projections. Relative to a dense hidden-width-64 neural readout, this reduces the feature-to-hidden parameter count from $64TnF$ to $d(T+n+F)+64d^3$, giving a $12.1\times$ feature-block compression at $T=50$, $n=6$, $d=8$, and $F=n+\binom{n}{2}$. Across Mackey-Glass forecasting and TFIM phase classification, ML-QRC remains statistically competitive with Ridge on Mackey-Glass and obtains the numerically highest full-data TFIM accuracy among tested methods, while using $12.0\times$ fewer parameters than the full dense MLP. Its clearest benefit is improved low-data stability relative to neural MLP readouts on Mackey-Glass; this advantage does not transfer to TFIM, where Ridge performs best at 50\% data. Overall, ML-QRC is best viewed as a tensor-structured neural readout that compresses dense MLP readouts while preserving QRC tensor structure, rather than as a replacement for simple linear/Ridge readouts in the tested regime.

title: On the Fast Electrons-Optical Modes Interaction Problem Error
abstract:
arXiv:2610.13976v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A recently developed relativistic quantum optics approach for a fast electron beam-optical modes interaction problem (Optica 6, 1524--1534 (2019)) contains suggestion about a smallness of the error induced by replacement $\Psi_{\vec k}\approx\Psi_{\vec k_0}$ for noninteracting free electron Dirac spinors at such wave vector $\vec k$ that $\left|\vec k-\vec k_0 \right| \ll\left|\vec k_0\right|$ with $\vec k_0$ as a peaked wave vector of a focused electron beam. Here, based on quantum information approach we strictly investigated a degree of coincidence of spinors $\Psi_{\vec k}$ and $\Psi_{\vec k_0}$ by calculating fidelity for them. The analytical expression is obtained. It is shown that the fidelity inevitably depends on not only wave vectors $\vec k$ and $\vec k_0$ but also on mutual orientation of $[\vec k_0,\vec k]$ and $\hat{\vec{s}}^{\dagger}\vec{\sigma}\hat{\vec{s}}$ with $\vec{s}$ is a two-component spin unit vector and $\vec{\sigma}$ is a vector of Pauli matrices. This result can be conceived as a chirality-like effect in the fidelity and constraints spin arbitrariness when applying the developed relativistic quantum optics approach to the problems of interest. A geometrical configuration of $\vec k_0$, $\vec k-\vec k_0$, and $\hat{\vec{s}}^{\dag}\vec\sigma\hat{\vec{s}}$ that is optimal in terms of fidelity is established.

title: Energy, Passivity, and Diffusive Representations in Anisotropic Fractional Maxwell--Cole--Cole Media
abstract:
arXiv:2610.13985v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This study develops an energy formulation for linear anisotropic Maxwell--Cole--Cole media with multiple fractional polarization channels, passive conductivity, prescribed currents, and finite-terminal Caputo memory with zero prehistory. A weighted solution class captures the integrable fractional initial layer generated by quiescent polarization. Fractional polarization power then separates into a nonnegative history storage and a nonnegative constitutive dissipation rate. Although the instantaneous rate may diverge at initialization, it remains integrable, while stored history energy and accumulated loss vanish initially. Combined with the Poynting theorem, this decomposition yields a global field-plus-memory identity that establishes electromagnetic passivity, closed-system energy decay, and conditional uniqueness under zero-supply boundary conditions. The framework also recovers the Debye, instantaneous-dielectric, vanishing-susceptibility, and vacuum limits under convergence assumptions. A positive diffusive representation provides a second decomposition whose storage never exceeds the history storage. Their difference is an exact nonnegative weighted variance that vanishes only for a zero polarization history. In agreement with these time-domain results, the finite-time harmonic response approaches the anisotropic multichannel Cole--Cole permittivity, whose Hermitian imaginary part ensures nonnegative cycle-averaged absorption. A reproducible single-channel study shows that fractional order broadens the dielectric-loss band, redistributes wave attenuation, strengthens the integrable initial power layer, and prolongs the step-response tail. An exact electric-step response verifies both energy representations. The formulation connects fractional initial layers, hereditary storage, passivity, diffusive relaxation, dispersion, absorption, and attenuation in a local constitutive model.

title: SIREN: A nonlinear Rankine-source boundary element solver for the stationary motion of a marine vehicle in calm water
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14027v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: SIREN (Ship Inviscid Resistance and Elevation eNgine) is a Rankine-source panel solver for the steady wave resistance of a ship, in the tradition of Dawson's method. The free-surface condition is linearised about a base flow, and the linearisation is iterated. In the present formulation the base flow is the solution of a Neumann problem on the actual boundary: sources on the entire hull, wet and dry, and on the free surface panels, with impermeability imposed on both, so that the free surface acts as a rigid lid at the position it currently occupies. This replaces the classical double-body flow, whose image about z=0 is meaningful only for a flat surface and a hull cut at z=0, and it removes the need for desingularised free-surface panels. In the non-linear iteration the free-surface panels are moved rigidly in the vertical to the relaxed wave elevation at their centroid, the hull panels are marked wet or dry against the moved surface, and the base flow is recomputed on the moved geometry; impermeability applies to the whole hull regardless of this marking, which is used only to select which panels enter the force integral, and under-relaxation is confined to the passes where the non-linear correction accumulates without being reset. The radiation condition is imposed by a one-row upstream shift of the collocation points, and the wave resistance is obtained by pressure integration and, independently, by transverse wave-cut analysis.

title: A Gauge-Inspired Coupled Fokker--Planck System for Multistate Stochastic Dynamics: Formalism and 1-D Numerical Implementation
authors: Francesco Pio De Cosmo, Gianluca Di Natale, Leandro Cieri
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14052v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Extending the Fokker--Planck equation to a coupled system of equations through non-Abelian symmetry groups offers a powerful theoretical framework for coupled multi-state stochastic systems. However, translating this abstract gauge field formulation into viable numerical predictions remains an unaddressed challenge. Motivated by our previous work on ice crystal habit evolution, in this work we bridge this gap by presenting the first numerical solver for an SU(2) gauge-coupled Fokker--Planck system in (1+1) dimensions. Using an operator-splitting scheme combined with a non-oscillatory advection solver, our algorithm strictly ensures probability conservation, non-negativity, and numerical stability. We demonstrate that non-Abelian gauge coupling acts as a cross-reactive feedback loop that fundamentally alters system dynamics, driving continuous probability exchange between states, suppressing localised density peaks, and forcing long-time spatial delocalisation. Validated across linear and quadratic coupling regimes up to strong interactions (g <= 1.0), this work establishes the foundational computational infrastructure needed to integrate complex multi-state physics. Overall, while our approach provides a key step toward improving ice cloud representation in atmospheric and climate models, the underlying physical framework and computational engine remain fundamentally general and multidisciplinary, offering a versatile paradigm for any domain requiring coupled multi-state stochastic equations.

title: acousticHelmholtzFoam: an MPI-parallel unstructured finite-volume solver for frequency-domain acoustics in heterogeneous two-phase media with perfectly matched layers
authors: Chuanchao Xu, Jun Liu, Dieter Bothe, Tomislav Maric
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14057v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: acousticHelmholtzFoam is an OpenFOAM application that computes time-harmonic acoustic pressure fields in heterogeneous gas-liquid media on unstructured polyhedral meshes. The complex pressure is stored as real and imaginary volume fields, the material coefficients are constructed from a volume-of-fluid phase fraction with geometric face-fraction averaging, and open boundaries are truncated by Cartesian perfectly matched layers (PMLs) whose damping tensor is generated by the companion utility setPMLFields. The two coupled real-valued equations are discretized with the cell-centred finite-volume operators of OpenFOAM and assembled explicitly, including processor couplings and boundary contributions, into a distributed PETSc matrix that is solved by default with the MUMPS sparse direct solver. The solver writes pressure amplitude, complex velocity, acoustic radiation pressure and time-averaged momentum flux for acoustic-force evaluation. This paper documents the implemented equations, the case interface, the assembly and solution algorithm, the build procedure and the test infrastructure. A layered gas-liquid-PML case with an analytical solution serves as an end-to-end regression: on 8000 cells the whole-domain relative complex-pressure error is $1.197\times10^{-3}$, and serial and MPI solutions on up to eight ranks agree to within $10^{-12}$ in relative $L_2$ norm. A single-axis acoustic-levitator height sweep with constant-volume spheroidal drops demonstrates the two-phase material input and the force output, and strong- and problem-size-scaling measurements characterize the direct-solver workflow. The numerical formulation and its verification are presented in a companion paper (arXiv:2610.01593).

title: Can the Quantum Fisher Effective Dimension Judge a Hybrid Quantum Neural Network?
authors: Md Masum Mia, Amith Khandakar, Mohamed Arselene Ayari
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14070v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hybrid quantum neural networks (QNNs) pair a classical feature extractor with a variational quantum circuit, and the effective dimension of the circuit's quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) is widely used to assess such models. This scalar is often interpreted as an indicator of trainability or accuracy, although these readings are rarely tested under controlled conditions. We therefore investigate what it actually measures. We define the effective dimension as the participation ratio of the QFIM diagonal, which lies between one and the parameter count, and we evaluate it across two image datasets, four frozen backbones including a random-projection control, four circuit depths on eight qubits, and three seeds. During training, the effective dimension remains well below the parameter count, and its correlation with test accuracy ranges from -0.72 to +0.87, changing sign across seeds in half of the configurations. Increasing depth activates a larger share of the circuit directions, from 0.38 to 0.91 of the parameter count, while the initialization gradient variance remains between 1e-5 and 1e-4, so no barren plateau (BP) appears at eight qubits. At a fixed circuit, the four backbones share an initial effective dimension of 6 to 9, even though CIFAR-10 accuracy ranges from 23.14% to 86.44%. These results show that the effective dimension characterizes circuit geometry rather than model quality. We conclude with a practical protocol that assigns each diagnostic to the question it can answer.

title: Prelocality No-Go Theorems and Exactly Solvable Relational History Hamiltonians
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14081v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Exact permutation covariance does not itself supply a sparse metric geometry. For permutation-covariant, full-support $k$-body interaction orbits, the incident interaction norm scales as $\binom{N-1}{k-1}|J_N|\|h\|$; such orbits cannot have uniformly finite range in metrics of diverging diameter. A permutation-invariant Hamiltonian diagonal in the graph basis has ground-state multiplicity at least $N!/|\mathrm{Aut}(G)|$ whenever $G$ is a ground graph. We give a quantitative version for approximately symmetric energies, together with fixed-radius connectivity and unitary-isometry obstructions. The trace-distance asymmetry of an arbitrary state also bounds its probability of selecting one labeled graph.
  We then construct two exactly solvable finite relational history Hamiltonians. A cyclic clock with a reversible incidence update has a unique ground state; gauge reduction yields a cycle Laplacian with a rank-one pin and the exact gap $\Delta_{N,L}=E_* (1-\cos\theta_L)$, where $\tan(L\theta_L/2)=1/\sin\theta_L$ and $0<\theta_L<\pi/L$. In particular, $\Delta_{N,L}/E_*=\pi^2/(2L^2)-2\pi^2/L^3+O(L^{-4})$, independently of the number of vertices. In an alternative order-free architecture, one clock qubit per unordered pair gives commuting four-local terms, $2^N$ ground states and a size-independent gap $E_*(1-1/\sqrt2)$. A fixed-weight control penalty selects $\binom Nq$ ground states without reducing the gap. These exact finite results expose clock and locality resource tradeoffs; they do not establish an emergent geometric phase.

title: How long is a photon?
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14088v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A photon has the strange property that it travels along a null interval with zero proper time, hence its emission and absorption points are, in a sense, a singular event. For their part, the emission and absorption processes have a finite duration which determines the spectral content of the photon. The question in the title points to the conceptual difficulty in `stitching' together these three intervals, which all correspond to the same physical entity but have fundamentally incompatible temporal descriptions. A previously developed model for quantum wavefunction propagation solves this apparent dilemma by formulating the life cycle of a photon in terms of recursive Fourier transforms on dual spaces. Because it doesn't treat space as dependent on time, and it is built on the Fourier transform whose phase is an invariant in special relativity as well as the foundation of the uncertainty principle, the model is a promising candidate framework for making quantum mechanics compatible with relativity. The model proposes to serve as an improved Klein-Gordon equation, or relativistically compatible replacement for Schr\"{o}dinger's equation.

title: Comment on "Landau Levels and Riemann Zeros"
authors: Mi-Ra Hwang, Eylee Jung, MuSeong Kim, DaeKil Park
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14108v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sierra and Townsend (ST) [1] showed that the ``absorption spectrum'' model of Connes [2] arises as the lowest-Landau-level (LLL) limit of a charged particle in crossed electric and magnetic fields, and suggested that the higher Landau levels supply the fluctuation part of the Riemann-zero counting function $N(E)$. Within the approximation used by ST we construct the eigenfunctions of an arbitrary Landau level $n$ and derive their asymptotics at the two box boundaries that ST identify. The boundary condition is the same as for $n=0$ up to an $E$-independent phase $(-\ii)^n$, so no $\ln E$ term arises for any fixed $n$. We also note that the $\ln E$ term in the semiclassical Eq.~(29) of ST is the first-order shift of the smooth LLL counting function, $E\to E+\gamma z^2$.

title: Additional ionization during nuclear $\beta^{\pm}$ decay in atomic systems
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14109v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An original method is developed for numerical calculations of probabilities of the bound-free atomic excitations during the nuclear $\beta^{\pm}$ decays in actual atoms and ions. To achieve this goal we have derived and tested the closed analytical formulas for the final state probabilities of different excitations in the few-electron atomic systems. This study is the first non-approximate and essentially complete investigation of the atomic bound-free excitations during the nuclear $\beta^{\pm}$ decays in atoms.

title: Hamiltonian-Dependent Compressibility and Physical Preservation in Approximate Quantum Compilation using Tensor Networks
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14125v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Approximate quantum compilation (AQC) using tensor networks provides a promising route to reducing the circuit resources required for quantum simulation. However, the factors governing the compressibility of many-body dynamics and the extent to which compressed circuits retain physically relevant information on quantum hardware remain poorly understood. We investigate these questions using AQCtensor for an 80-qubit one-dimensional anisotropic XYZ Heisenberg chain initialized in a N\'eel state. By varying the exchange anisotropy and external magnetic field, we find that compression performance changes systematically with the anisotropic coupling configuration and field orientation. These variations are strongly associated with a nested-commutator measure related to second-order Trotter error, with corresponding directional trends also reflected in the target-state MPS bond dimension. For an 80-qubit quantum-hardware evaluation, AQCtensor compresses a 10-repetition target evolution to 5 repetitions while retaining a target-state fidelity of 0.995474, reducing the total circuit depth by 45.9% and the two-qubit gate count by 47.6%. The compressed circuit exhibits comparable behavior across magnetization, nearest-neighbor correlation, and Hamiltonian expectation measurements, while process-level diagnostics and local reduced-state tomography provide complementary characterization beyond these observables. Together, these results link AQCtensor compressibility to Hamiltonian commutator structure and target-state complexity and demonstrate substantial circuit reduction while retaining physically relevant features in an 80-qubit quantum-hardware experiment.

title: Spatial Nonlocality from Finite Extinction Ratio in BOTDR over Heterogeneous Fiber Links
authors: Giannis Poulopoulos, Constantinos Haliotis, Panagiotis Toumasis, Hercules Avramopoulos
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14128v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Finite extinction ratio in pulse-modulated Brillouin optical time-domain reflectometry (BOTDR) produces residual inter-pulse Brillouin backscatter outside the nominal pulse gate. We model and experimentally quantify this effect as spatial nonlocality in a heterogeneous fiber link and define the spectral contamination ratio (SCR) as the contaminating Brillouin-band power normalized to the local Brillouin-band power. Measurements were performed using a 1.2 km standard single-mode fiber (SMF) followed by 0.1 km of dispersion-compensating fiber (DCF), whose separated Brillouin frequency shifts allow section-to-section leakage to be resolved spectrally. At 20 m spatial resolution, increasing the extinction ratio from 18.5 to 33.0 dB reduced the SMF-band contamination in the DCF gates from -5.3 to -14.8 dB. Over the 16-33 dB range, the SCR showed fitted slopes of -1.064 and -1.246 dB/dB for the two contamination directions. These results quantify finite-ER-induced spatial nonlocality and provide a link-specific metric for extinction-ratio selection in BOTDR.

title: IceCube data for astrophysical neutrinos exhibit q-statistical behavior
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14129v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Relevant IceCube recent data for astrophysical neutrinos are analyzed. Similarly to cosmic rays and proton-proton LHC collisions, the corresponding spectra are satisfactorily described, for the entire interval of measured energies, through q-Gaussians. This fact reinforces the already available evidence that nonadditive entropies (either of the $S_q$ class or of the $S_{delta}$ one, or even alternative ones) appear to play a crucial role in systems such as black holes and related cosmological phenomena (e.g., dark energy). The IceCube data yield sensibly high values for the momenta-distribution nonadditive index (q \simeq 1.6), in contrast with the cosmic rays values (q \simeq 1.2) and the LHC values (q \simeq 1.1). This fact neatly indicates very-long-ranged space-time correlations. The detailed associated physical mechanisms remain, at the present stage, as an instigating open issue.

title: Diverging paths to dark-matter discovery
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14137v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The scientific discovery of dark matter has been pursued in two very different methodological and epistemic contexts. A microphysical context centered around the laboratory detection of a new particle, and a macrophysical context based on the astronomical identification of a non-luminous gravitating component. The justification for the salience of methodological diversity is that these different methods are complementary ways to discovering aspects of the same entity. The weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) made this expectation scientifically credible by connecting a particle candidate to a cosmological abundance, experimental searches, and explanations of astronomical phenomena. What happens to this connection when the WIMP loses its central position? I analyze 201,627 NASA Astrophysics Data System records to examine the organization of research following the decline of WIMP prominence. Astrophysics and high-energy physics remain jointly dominant, while WIMP-related mentions decline in both fields and successor candidates receive different degrees of attention. Concept networks show that WIMP-related research remains central across the literature, even as cross-field connections become less concentrated around it. These indicators measure research attention; they do not establish what scientists would accept as a discovery. I interpret the findings through a framework distinguishing constitutive identification, cosmic attribution, explanatory adequacy, and the cross-domain identification needed to connect them. A particle, compact-object population, or gravitational theory can resolve different parts of the inherited problem, and a partial or multicomponent discovery can leave other parts open. 'Diverging paths' describes this branching of possible resolutions.

title: Categorifying Quantum Spin Systems
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14165v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We develop a homotopical framework for understanding the space of quantum spin systems based on topological $n$-nets, which assign associative unital algebras to local regions in an $n$-dimensional space in a manner that captures the locality structure of the underlying lattice theories. The net-theoretic perspective admits a natural categorification, in which the category of topological $n$-nets carries the structure of a higher Morita category. Moreover, the nets of greatest physical interest form a Karoubi-complete subcategory that shares many of the characteristic structural features of the category of finite TQFTs. Our main result identifies the group of locality-preserving symmetries of (3+1)-dimensional quantum spin systems (i.e. quantum cellular automata modulo stabilization, finite-depth quantum circuits, and translations) with the full Witt group of nondegenerate braided fusion categories, thereby answering a question posed by Haah.

title: Compass in the Mirror: Quantum Backpropagation with the Hopf Ansatz
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14177v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A variational quantum state may have many control angles, and its complete gradient contains one derivative for each. The task is to turn access to selected derivatives into a shared finite-shot record for the complete vector. The Hopf ansatz supplies the setting: it constructs any normalized pure state from nested two-way magnitude splits and, for complex states, leaf phases, with one directly programmed angle per split or phase. Earlier Hopf constructions prepare the state, recover coordinates from known amplitudes, and provide indexed derivative access. With a phase-calibrated controlled reflection, the inverse Hopf frame maps each normalized magnitude direction to a computational label, so every all-$X$ outcome contributes to every magnitude derivative. A separate signed leaf record supplies the complex phase block. A checkpoint variant reverses only the suffix below a selected depth and returns that layer's gradient block. For a complete chart with $M$ real-valued parameters, sufficient execution counts are $\mathcal{O}(\log\log M)$ for the global method and $\mathcal{O}(\log M\log\log M)$ for the complete checkpoint schedule at fixed additive coordinate accuracy and confidence. The global saving is record reuse, not a reduction of the $M$-entry output. Under the designated direct-angle schedules, the global method's assigned Hopf CNOT work and input/output-inclusive storage have at most logarithmic overhead relative to a matched scalar evaluation. The same Hopf geometry thus carries a state forward and the objective's complete coordinate response backward.

title: Lifting an $[n,k,d]$ Binary Linear Code to an $[[n,k,d]]$ Quantum Stabilizer Code
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14192v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The codeword stabilized (CWS) framework provides a systematic method for constructing quantum error correcting codes from a simple undirected graph and a classical code. When the underlying classical code is linear, the resulting quantum code is a stabilizer code. In this work, we investigate the conditions under which an arbitrary $[n,k,d]$ classical binary linear code can be lifted to an $[[n,k,d]]$ quantum stabilizer code using the CWS framework. We analyze the random CWS code constructed from a given $[n,k,d]$ binary linear code $\mathcal{C}$ and an Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi random graph $\mathrm{G}(n, \frac12)$. We establish a lower bound on the probability that the resulting quantum code preserves the minimum distance $d$ of the classical code. This probabilistic analysis yields a Gilbert-Varshamov-type condition on the $n,k,d$ parameters of the classical code that guarantees the existence of a graph resulting in a quantum code with the same $n,k,d$ parameters.

title: Below-threshold execution of fault-tolerant ripple-carry addition on a trapped-ion quantum computer
authors: Jacob S. Nelson, Andrew J. Landahl, Andrew D. Baczewski
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14202v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We deploy a universal fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) architecture based on error-detecting $[\![8,3,2]\!]$ and $[\![4,2,2]\!]$ codes on Quantinuum's Helios-1 trapped-ion quantum computer. We compile and execute ripple-carry adder (RCA) circuits for classical inputs up to five bits on this architecture. Uncomputing a workspace qubit provides an additional ``algorithmic check'' to detect errors. While available at both the physical and logical levels, this check synergizes with our architecture by increasing the effective fault distance of many circuit locations from two to four. Combining this algorithmic check with the error-detecting codes, we observed only a single logical failure in one-bit addition after burst-error filtering, yielding an estimated logical failure rate of $(6.0 \pm 5.9) \times 10^{-5}$. This is well below the $(3.5 \pm 1.3) \times 10^{-3}$ failure probability observed for one-bit addition on the same hardware in unencoded form. Two- and three-bit adders also showed performance improvements, while the longer four- and five-bit adders executed just above threshold.

title: An Introduction to the $p$-Differential Forms in Spinor Variables on the Minkowskian Manifold
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14240v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This article presents an introductory study of $p$-differential forms in spinor variables defined on the Minkowskian (or Lorentzian) manifold. Starting from the algebraic and geometric foundations of spinor spaces and Clifford algebras, we establish the correspondence between Minkowski spacetime and Hermitian matrices in spinor coordinates. Within this framework, we construct differential 1-forms and 2-forms expressed in spinor notation, and formulate the Dirac operator in terms of exterior calculus. Furthermore, we extend this approach to the case of non-monogenic functions, following the method proposed in~\cite{Jaramillo2024}. The results illustrate the consistency of the spinorial exterior calculus and its potential applications in the study of relativistic field equations and geometric formulations of quantum theory.

title: Quantum Signal Processing Phase Factorization via Logarithmic Derivatives
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14259v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum signal processing (QSP) requires the efficient computation of phase factors associated with a polynomial transformation. One existing stable factorization method avoids direct root finding but relies on Prony's method to recover a polynomial from weighted power sums of its roots (arXiv:2202.02671). We present a modification of this approach that eliminates Prony's method by using the logarithmic derivative of an associated polynomial. Because the logarithmic derivative has the same residue at every root after accounting for multiplicity, its Fourier coefficients directly yield the unweighted power sums of the roots inside the unit disk. The Newton--Girard identities then recover the coefficients of the corresponding polynomial without computing its roots. The resulting algorithm has $O(d\log^2 d)$ computational complexity and simplifies the factorization procedure of the original method. In numerical experiments on Hamiltonian simulation, eigenstate filtering, matrix inversion, and the Fermi--Dirac operator, our implementation computes phase factors in seconds with maximum errors on the order of $10^{-12}$.

title: Definition of Multi-Parameter Super-Resolution for Optical Telescopes
authors: Peter Menart, Seungman Choi, Zubin Jacob
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14286v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Super-resolution techniques in microscopy are opening new frontiers in biology, and super-resolution for telescope imaging may provide similar benefits for astronomy and space domain awareness. Telescope super-resolution techniques such as multi-plane light conversion and photonic lanterns have been inspired by the ability of mode sorting measurements to extract classical Fisher information closer to the quantum bound than standard telescope imaging. Fisher information analyses for super-resolution imaging systems commonly consider the case of imaging point sources, but often only consider estimating a small subset of the parameters. Furthermore, there has been no demonstration of an estimation algorithm with performance that follows the limit set by the Fisher information when all point source parameters are considered. We provide a framework for defining and analyzing super-resolution using the classical and quantum Fisher information for the multi-parameter estimation problem and demonstrate an algorithm that can achieve the classical Fisher information bound for all the parameters simultaneously.

title: Fast local field calculation in cascaded coupled systems
authors: Isam Ben Soltane, Romain Asso, Matthieu Davy
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14314v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Computing the field within a sub-unit of cascaded systems is a recurring problem in wave physics. It is central to gradient-based inverse design, in situations where only a region of the system is modified while the rest remains fixed. Standard approaches either resimulate the entire cascade at every change, or require a detailed characterization of every surrounding sub-system. Both become impractical when many design iterations are needed. Here, we introduce a hybrid method combining the $S$-matrix approach, which propagates fields through cascaded systems, with the Green's function method, which gives the field generated by a source within a characterized system. In this approach, the sub-systems surrounding the region of interest need only be characterized once, after which the local field can be recomputed rapidly for any new configuration. We validate the method on a disordered lossy waveguide, finding excellent agreement with finite-element simulations. We also demonstrate its efficiency on a disordered multimode cavity, where it achieves a fifty-fold speed-up over full-wave simulation and reduces a wideband focusing calculation from eleven hours to ten minutes. This approach opens the way to fast, iterative field calculations in complex systems coupled to their environment, with direct applications to inverse design and wideband wavefront-shaping.

title: Inverse Resonance Problem for the Half-Line Schr\"odinger Operator with a Complex Robin Boundary Condition
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14323v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study the inverse resonance problem for the one-dimensional Schr\"odinger operator on the half-line with a compactly supported complex-valued potential and a complex Robin boundary condition \[ u'(0)-a u(0)=0,\qquad a\in\mathbb C. \] The proof follows the transformation-operator, entire-function, and Fourier analytic strategy developed by Marletta, Shterenberg and Weikard for the Dirichlet problem \cite{MSW}. The Dirichlet Jost function $\psi(z,0)$ is replaced by the Robin characteristic function \[ F_a(z;q)=\psi_x(z,0;q)-a\psi(z,0;q). \] We establish the corresponding large-energy estimates, Hadamard factorization, finite-data stability, and uniqueness results. The principal new feature is that $F_a(z;q)=iz-a+O(1)$ rather than $1+O(z^{-1})$. In the transformation-operator argument the relevant boundary quantity is $B_x(0,t)-aB(0,t)$, together with the scalar term $B(0,0)$. For fixed $a\in\mathbb C$, and uniformly for $a$ in bounded subsets of $\mathbb C$, the resulting inverse resonance estimates have the same qualitative form as those proved in \cite{MSW} for the Dirichlet problem. In particular, for a fixed Robin parameter $a$, the complete set of Robin eigenvalues and resonances, counted with multiplicity, determines the potential uniquely.
  The text is produced with the help of AI ChatGPT for Academy.

title: Competitive scaling of small-subsystem-optimization heuristics for LABS
authors: Ginger E. Lau, Adil A. Gangat
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14361v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The low autocorrelation binary sequences (LABS) problem, often formulated as a spin-lattice energy-minimization problem, is a combinatorial optimization problem with a very rugged energy landscape. We demonstrate that iterative optimization of very small subsystems of n spins that are decoupled from the rest of the system achieves global optimization of LABS with a time-to-solution scaling that is competitive with heuristics that optimize the global system of N spins directly. Our isolated-subsystem heuristic with n = 4 achieves a time scaling of O(1.333N ) on the interval N = [27, 60], while the current state-of-the-art classical and quantum scalings are respectively O(1.34N ) and O(1.21N ). Our results suggest that specialized optimization hardware with only small numbers of logical spins may be of practical relevance.

title: The GHZ Game in Black and White
authors: Terry Rudolph, Tony Newton, Dan-Adrian German
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14411v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We show that it is possible for three people to win the GHZ game with just the standard real valued misty state formalism, but each party will need to have two balls instead of one. That is, there will be six balls involved, rather than three. In fact, as a general rule, instead of using complex numbers in a quantum computer you can always add a qubit to "tag" complex numbers. But for proofs of non-locality, like the GHZ game, we cannot have a single universal tagging qubit, because all three parties would need access to it and therefore they could potentially transfer information via it. That's where we need to replace the one ball with three that each only need to be accessed locally.

title: Yang-Mills Theory in the Multisymplectic Framework
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14418v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This Master's thesis develops and applies the multisymplectic field-theory framework to (pure) Yang-Mills theory. Building from the geometric foundations of jet bundles and the Poincar\'e-Cartan forms, the work constructs the Lagrangian multisymplectic formalism for first-order field theories, recovering the usual Euler-Lagrange field equations and extending the Poisson brackets of symplectic mechanics to a full graded Lie algebra. It then establishes the Legendre correspondence with the multisymplectic Hamiltonian formalism (in which Hamilton equations are retrieved) including the case of singular Lagrangians (where a constraint algorithm is reproduced). Breaking Lorentz covariance via a Cauchy surface slicing, the thesis then relates the covariant multisymplectic picture to an instantaneous presymplectic (infinite-dimensional) formulation in which the instantaneous De Donder equations and presymplectic brackets are obtained in a compatible way. A comprehensive treatment of symmetries then leads to multisymplectic and instantaneous momentum maps generalizations and to several versions of Noether's theorems.
  Specializing the formalism to principal-bundle gauge theory, the thesis identifies the multisymplectic configuration space with the bundle of connections, gauge symmetries with symmetries in the multisymplectic language and builds the Yang-Mills Lagrangian. Lastly, among many computations, the standard tensorial Yang-Mills equations and the Bianchi identity in local trivializations are retrieved, Yang-Mills conserved currents and charges are obtained and the graded algebra is derived for a special class of Hamiltonian forms.

title: Exponential Quantum Advantage in Stationary Signal Sensing
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14424v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sensing time-varying signals is essential for precision measurement and for characterizing fluctuations in physical systems. In this work, we show that quantum entanglement provides an exponential advantage in the acquisition time required to learn the temporal statistics of a stationary classical signal. The task is to estimate the characteristic function of joint displacements on selected bosonic modes within a fixed-duration window, using continuous measurements of one signal realization. We present an entanglement-assisted scheme based on two-mode squeezed probes and local Bell measurements with protected idlers, and bound its acquisition time accounting for readout noise and correlations between signal windows. For a strictly stationary pulse family, it achieves polynomial acquisition time at inverse-polynomial accuracy with logarithmic squeezing and polynomial photon number. On the other hand, we prove that any local idler-free protocols require acquisition time exponential in the number of selected temporal modes per window. This lower bound holds for both sequentially prepared and arbitrarily temporally entangled probes, allowing non-Gaussian inputs and measurements and causal classical feedback, as long as each output is measured destructively within its time bin. These results establish an exponential quantum learning advantage for a single continuously monitored stationary signal, with the sensing cost measured by total acquisition time.

title: Hyperpolarization-enabled cooperative molecular magnetic amplification
authors: Jingyan Xu, Raphael Kircher, Min Jiang, Xinhua Peng, Danila Barskiy, Dmitry Budker
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14425v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Detecting weak magnetic fields at hertz frequencies is central to biomagnetism, geophysical sensing, and searches for new physics, yet it remains challenging because of technical systematics and environmental noise. Here, we realize a continuously operating molecular magnetic amplifier. Signal amplification by reversible exchange (SABRE) parahydrogen-based hyperpolarization maintains non-equilibrium spin order at zero field, turning scalar-coupled nuclear spins in liquid state molecules into an active, frequency-selective gain medium. Measurements of its complex magnetic susceptibility ($\chi$) reveal an intrinsic response of $ | \chi | \approx$ 10. By feeding the collectively generated magnetic field back to the spins below the threshold for self-sustained $J$-oscillation, we extend the effective spin coherence and cooperatively enhance the susceptibility up to $ | \chi | \approx$ 80. Near threshold, this produces approximately fourfold amplification of a weak (20 pT) magnetic field at 3.37 Hz at the sensor location. These results establish hyperpolarized molecules as a tunable active magnetic medium for narrowband quantum sensing and precision measurement.

title: Quadrature-detected zero-to-ultralow-field nuclear magnetic resonance
authors: Anne M. Fabricant, Florin Teleanu, Adam Ortmeier, Piotr Put, Seth Dilday, Alexej Jerschow, Dmitry Budker, Thomas Theis, Danila A. Barskiy
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14451v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present the concept of quadrature-detected zero-to-ultralow-field nuclear magnetic resonance (QD ZULF NMR). Two orthogonal sensors, atomic optically pumped magnetometers, are used to separately detect components of oscillating sample magnetization, which are then combined into a quadrature signal. This approach enables the distinction of positive and negative resonance frequencies with respect to the laboratory frame---such that absolute signs of gyromagnetic ratios can be determined. In addition, QD ZULF NMR reduces peak density and overlap compared to ZULF NMR with single-axis detection, while providing richer information about nuclear-spin dynamics. As an illustration, we present experimental $J$-spectra for thermally polarized [$^{13}$C]-formic acid and [$^{13}$C]-methanol, compounds commonly used in ZULF NMR which represent XA and XA$_3$ spin systems, respectively. A theoretical framework describing QD ZULF NMR signals is provided.

title: Quantum-Fisher-information-aware optimization yields a quantum reservoir advantage over tuned classical reservoirs
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14454v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We show that a quantum reservoir computer optimized with its quantum Fisher information (QFI) has a quantum advantage over a classical reservoir of equal readout cost, provided by a quantum-information advantage: optimizing the quantum parameters with the QFI metric. On Mackey-Glass forecasting, a driven Jaynes-Cummings reservoir with one to three atoms beats a tuned echo-state network at every size from 4 to 30 trained weights, by 25-69% in held-out error, and is ahead of 99.5% of 10,000 random networks. After grid and Bayesian searches saturate, the QFI-aware stage lowers the error by 29-51% at 12-30 weights, beyond equal-budget black-box search or classical-parameter gradients alone, and at 30 weights turns a loss into a win. We then derive a fundamental QFI bound on the first-order rate of change of the retrained loss and factorize the gap to this bound into five link efficiencies that identify the physical mechanism limiting optimization.

title: Harmonic Reduction of Spin-Coupled Grover Walks on Hypercubes via Quantum Bernoulli Noises
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14467v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We consider spin-coupled Grover walks on hypercubes within the framework of quantum Bernoulli noises (QBN). We identify parity-dependent harmonic subspaces generated by the central Hamming layers: in even dimension they give a fixed-point subspace, whereas in odd dimension the walk reduces on the harmonic subspace to an explicit eight-dimensional reduced dynamics. Using symmetric-group representation theory, we characterize the corresponding isotypic structure and determine the reduced spectrum. The harmonic reduction also yields explicit long-time probability behavior and shows that the resulting states may occupy an asymptotically vanishing fraction of the hypercube while still spanning its full Hamming diameter.

title: Fast continuous ion transport through X-junctions with low motional excitation for QCCD architectures
authors: Jie Xiao, Zhao Wang, Chenghong Zhu, Shiqiang Gao, Xin Wang, Fa Dai, Xu Wang
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14472v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Trapped ion quantum computing based on the quantum charge coupled device (QCCD) architecture uses functional zoning and ion transport to enable high fidelity computation and all to all qubit connectivity. As trapped ion quantum processing units (QPU) scale, 90{\deg} X-junction turns account for an increasing fraction of total transport time. Frequent junction crossings, therefore, make transport speed and final phonon excitation direct determinants of quantum algorithm execution efficiency. However, complex electric fields in X-junctions complicate waveform design, making it difficult to achieve high speed and low final phonon excitation simultaneously. Here, we develop a waveform design method for low-phonon-excitation high-speed X-junction(LHX-T) transport. It integrates low barrier pseudopotential channel design using multiple radio frequency (Multi-RF), multidimensional shortcut to adiabaticity dynamics, and constrained DC voltage optimization over the entire transport sequence. This framework connects waveform design, control, and computational validation, with smooth multichannel waveforms computed rapidly through a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker(KKT) linear system. The resulting waveform transports a single $^{171}Yb^+$ ion through a 90{\deg} turn in $5\mu s$ at an average speed of 14.6 m/s. Over 50 consecutive round trips, the final equivalent coherent phonon number consistently stays below 0.001, with no noticeable accumulation over time. System level evaluations at the QCCD scale show that the median duration of a single execution cycle is reduced by about $30\%$ across various circuit types. The fraction of execution time spent on transport decreases from approximately $70\%$ to $55\%$. This approach offers a means of designing fast ion transport waveforms with low phonon excitation for scalable QCCD based QPUs and provides a technical basis for efficient execution of quantum algorithms.

title: A Portable Optical Frequency Comb with Low Repetition-Rate Drift Based on "Optical Cubes"
authors: Zhendong Chen, Hanbo Xu, Ruoao Yang, Tianyu Liu, Hongshuo Wu, Duo Pan, Zhigang Zhang, Jianjun Wu, Jingbiao Chen
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14490v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We demonstrate a compact, fully stabilized, all-polarization-maintaining (all-PM) Er:fiber optical frequency comb (OFC) implemented on a silica optical-cube platform. The optical comb module, including the oscillator, amplifier, spectral-broadening stage, 780-nm frequency-doubling branch, and f-to-2f interferometer, occupies a volume of 0.88 L. Without active temperature control, the free-running repetition frequency exhibits a peak-to-peak excursion of 75 Hz over 10 h, corresponding to 0.375 ppm. Under the same laboratory conditions, this excursion is 6.2 times smaller than that of a mechanically mounted non-PM reference comb. The amplified pulses are compressed to 94 fs and spectrally broadened in a PM highly nonlinear fiber. A coherent-population-trapping-based chip-scale atomic clock is employed for the first time as the radio-frequency reference for comb locking, thereby reducing the footprint of the microwave-reference subsystem. The resulting in-loop, optical-frequency-normalized tracking instability reaches 6.03E-17 at 1 s and 2.57E-18 at 10,000 s. These results demonstrate a compact comb architecture with reduced sensitivity to environmental perturbations, providing a practical route toward portable optical atomic clocks.

title: Sample-Size Scalability and Representation Sensitivity of Quantum Machine Learning Models for Higgs Boson Event Classification
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14533v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum machine learning offers new approaches to multivariate event classification in high-energy physics, but its performance relative to optimized classical methods remains uncertain under limited training data and restricted quantum resources. We investigate the sample-size scalability and representation sensitivity of a quantum support vector machine and a variational quantum classifier for Higgs-boson signal--background discrimination using simulated events from the ATLAS Higgs Machine Learning Challenge. The models are trained on balanced subsets ranging from 250 to 4000 events and evaluated on held-out samples preserving the original class distribution. Principal component analysis (PCA) and autoencoder (AE) representations are examined to reduce the input dimensionality and quantum-resource requirements. Four optimized classical classifiers are used as benchmarks under a common preprocessing, validation, and evaluation protocol. We assess training-sample scalability in classical and quantum classifiers using a four-component PCA representation and examine representation sensitivity through a secondary matched-event comparison of four- and eight-component PCA representations. Within the evaluated Higgs-boson classification setting, the QSVM showed stronger performance than the VQC at larger training sample sizes, while remaining below the best-performing classical classifiers.

title: Interpretation of chirality imprinted on photoelectron momentum spectra by three-dimensional light fields
authors: Junxin Yuan, Yuhong Li, Fei Li, Jinkai Zhang, Shiyang Zhong, Hao Teng, Yujun Yang, Yingchun Guo, Zhiyi Wei, Jing Chen, Xiaojun Liu, Bingbing Wang
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14557v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Synthetic three-dimensional (3D) light fields provide a new route to imprinting chirality on achiral matter through light--matter interaction. Although previous work has numerically demonstrated that chirality can be imprinted on the photoelectron momentum spectrum of atoms, a transparent analytical physical picture that links the structure of the driving field to the chirality of the spectrum is still an open question. Here, using frequency-domain theory based on nonperturbative quantum electrodynamics (QED), we demonstrate that this chirality originates from coherence between adjacent quantum transition channels. We further find that a symmetry transformation introduces into the coherence term a symmetry-breaking phase shift ($\Phi_{\mathrm{SBPS}}$), which can be tuned by varying the laser-field parameters to preserve or break the corresponding symmetry in the spectrum. Once all such symmetries are broken, the momentum spectrum becomes chiral. In particular, for the noncollinear two-color 3D light field considered here, the spectrum is chiral for even $f=\omega_2/\omega_1$ and achiral for odd $f$. Our results provide a microscopic interpretation of chirality imprinting and establish a framework for predicting and controlling chiral electron wave packets with synthetic 3D light fields.

title: Joint Trust-Distrust Structure Shapes Belief Propagation and Collective Dynamics
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14565v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Belief propagation in social networks depends on how trust and distrust jointly shape interpersonal influence. We develop a network model that treats trust and distrust as distinct but statistically coupled quantities. Their joint values determine the net trust and uncertainty of each relationship, and a neighbor can influence an agent only when both threshold conditions are satisfied. We show that the correlation between trust and distrust reshapes the transition between consensus and fragmentation by changing the availability of influential neighbors. Network connectivity also affects this transition, whereas degree heterogeneity has a more limited effect when networks have comparable mean degree. Moreover, the availability of influential neighbors alone does not determine the final consensus: correlations between relational properties and network degree can select agents with different degree compositions, altering the direction and magnitude of collective belief. Finally, we introduce a comfort index that quantifies the expected availability of influential neighbors and analytically links the joint trust-distrust structure to collective dynamics. Our results establish a mechanistic connection between relational structure, effective social influence, and emergent collective belief states.

title: Entanglement-Capability-Aware Finite-Bond Circuit Cutting for Distributed Quantum Computing
authors: Weidong Liu, Qingqing Jiang, Yufu Liu, Ruiqing He, Jiandong Shang, Hengliang Guo, Qiang Chen
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14580v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Distributed quantum computing distributes workloads that exceed a single processor's capacity across resource-constrained components. Circuit cutting enables this decomposition, but its effectiveness depends on partition choice. We present SACE, a Simulation-Aware Circuit Partitioning framework with Entanglement-Capability-Aware Screening. EP-Cost screens partitions using a parameter-dependent entanglement-capability proxy and native implementation cost. Under reconstruction constraints, finite-bond refinement selects the candidate that minimizes the worst-subcircuit discrepancy between normalized MPS simulations at bond dimensions $\chi$ and $2\chi$. Across 14 exhaustively enumerated small-scale candidate spaces, EP-Cost-guided genetic algorithm selections attain co-optimal native quasiprobability decomposition (QPD) overhead, with a median within-circuit Spearman correlation of 0.9965 between EP-Cost and QPD overhead. At matched cut counts, EP-Cost reduces QPD overhead by $25.20\times$ and $16.89\times$ for 8- and 9-qubit QFT circuits, respectively, and improves sampled reconstruction. On 12-qubit approximate QFT, deterministic reconstruction reduces Pauli-observable mean absolute error in all six low-bond conditions and total-variation distance in five. With five cuts and 7,776 QPD terms, SACE is best on all four reconstruction metrics in four of six conditions. At 24 qubits, SACE improves exact-local QFT accuracy in all 30 instance-bond-dimension conditions against each EP-Cost-only, Kernighan-Lin, and spectral baseline. The 50-qubit QFT comparisons remain favorable as reference convergence improves. Weighted QAOA circuits provide complementary, more bond-sensitive evidence. Refinement benefits persist across three search methods; larger candidate panels improve the optimized proxy without guaranteeing lower exact-local error.

title: Exploring Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions via the Dynamical Phase Accumulated at an Equilibrium Critical Point
authors: Han-Chuan Kou, Peng Li, Zhi-Han Zhang, Zhen-Yu Zheng
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14591v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We investigate dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) generated by a two-step linear quench with a finite waiting time at the equilibrium critical point. The waiting stage leads to the accumulation of a dynamical phase that depends on the waiting time and directly reflects the critical spectral structure. In the transverse Ising chain, this accumulated phase modifies the critical structure of DQPTs from a single-critical-mode (SCM) regime to a multiple-critical-mode (MCM) regime. We analytically and numerically determine the boundary between the two regimes. Along this boundary, the waiting time approaches a constant in the sudden-quench limit, whereas in the slow-quench limit it follows Kibble--Zurek (KZ) scaling with the quench time. In the SCM regime, the rate function exhibits a conventional linear singularity, $r(t)-r(t^{*})\propto |t-t^{*}|^\alpha$, with the critical exponent $\alpha=1$ near the critical time. At the SCM--MCM boundary, this exponent changes to $\alpha=1/2$, leading to a divergent first derivative of the rate function. Additional discrete parameter lines with $\alpha=1/2$ also appear within the MCM regime in the parameter plane spanned by the waiting and quench times. Our findings establish a direct connection between the accumulated dynamical phase and the critical structure of DQPTs, further supported by an extended Su--Schrieffer--Heeger (SSH) model.

title: Scalability and performance metrics for boson sampling devices
authors: Dong-Gil Im, Chung-Hyun Lee, Joonsuk Huh, Yoon-Ho Kim
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14602v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Linear-optical platforms provide a promising route to demonstrate quantum computational advantage, particularly through the boson sampling problem. While a boson sampling system should be large enough to show the quantum advantage, the size of the boson sampling problem is often restricted by experimental constraints. In particular, as a boson sampling system is scaled up, experimental constraints can limit its effective problem size to permit efficient classical simulation. In this paper, we investigate the theoretical scalability bounds for boson sampling systems under practical experimental conditions, including photon loss, mode mismatch, and input state error. We employ non-negativity conditions for phase-space quasiprobability distribution functions to analyze these effects. In addition, we introduce two device-level metrics, the boson sampling score which measures the usable capacity of a given device and the boson sampling volume which provides a common hardware-level benchmark for comparing different platforms and assessing their access to an advantage-relevant problem size regime. Our results provide fundamental insights into the performance of boson sampling systems under realistic experimental conditions and offer practical guidelines for scaling up boson sampling systems.

title: Maximal Axion Optical Chirality Enabled by Degenerate Quasibound States in the Continuum
authors: Chang-Yin Ji, Chong Wang, Jiafang Li, Yugui Yao
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14611v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Axion quasiparticles introduce magnetoelectric coupling in topological materials, yet their optical signatures are intrinsically weak, severely limiting experimental detection and practical exploitation. Here, we demonstrate maximal optical chirality of axion quasiparticles by coupling them with degenerate quasibound states in the continuum (qBICs). By integrating three-dimensional topological insulators (3DTIs) with achiral photonic crystal slabs (PCSs), we reveal that axion quasiparticles induce an effective Zeeman effect that lifts the degeneracy of achiral qBICs in PCSs, splitting them into two nondegenerate high-Q chiral qBICs with maximally opposite chirality. These result in a more than 10^3- and 200-fold increase in the polarization conversion efficiency and Faraday rotation angle, respectively, compared to the intrinsic chiroptical response of bare 3DTI films. Moreover, circular dichroism and nonreciprocal optical responses are revealed as new key signatures for probing axion quasiparticles in 3DTI-PCS coupled systems. Our results provide a definitive route for observing axion quasiparticles and topological physics, while establishing a promising platform for controlling optical polarization, spin, phase, and nonreciprocal responses.

title: Near-focus intensity evolution of spatiotemporal optical vortex pulses and consequences for their nonlinear upconversion
authors: Titouan Gadeyne, Vartika Vishnoi, Thierry Ruchon
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14640v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spatiotemporal optical vortex (STOV) laser pulses are attracting attention for their puzzling transverse orbital angular momentum (OAM) and propagation properties, which could determine their future applications. While the characteristic reshaping of their space-time envelope upon diffraction from the focal plane to the far-field is now well-established, the evolution of their intensity as they propagate has not been studied quantitatively, despite growing interest for their use in nonlinear optics and strong-field physics. Here, we explore experimentally and analytically the focusing dynamics of STOVs produced by a pulse shaper, and evidence a substantial longitudinal shift between the coordinate at which a circularly-symmetric STOV forms and that at which the pulse reaches its peak intensity. To illustrate some practical consequences for applications, we experimentally demonstrate how the yield of second-harmonic generation can consequently be maximized several Rayleigh lengths beyond the plane where the circular STOV really occurs. These results signal careful characterization of spatiotemporal pulses as a requisite for nonlinear optical experiments, and pave the way for finer control of complex laser drivers for light-matter interactions.

title: Reducing Trust Cost in Quantum Application Development Using AI
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14665v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative AI can be a powerful tool for supporting the design and implementation of quantum applications, whereas the burden of checking whether generated circuits realize the intended computation increases. In this study, we regard this burden of human understanding, checking, and judgment as ``trust cost,'' and propose a development methodology that integrates AI and formal verification to reduce it. In the proposed development methodology, the implementation is divided into three components: a target mathematical specification, a quantum circuit, and a correspondence theorem and its proof that prove the agreement between the two. This division separates the specifications and theorem statements checked by humans from the theorem proofs entrusted to mechanical checking. As a concrete development example of this proposal, we describe an implementation for the time evolution of a stochastic particle system and its results.

title: Selective spatiotemporal mode-locking in multimode Mamyshev oscillators
authors: Changfeng Wang, Jia Liu, Yutai Zhao, Ran Xia, Wenjun Ni, Chunyong Yang, Xiahui Tang, Gang Xu, Perry Ping Shum
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14690v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spatiotemporal mode-locking (STML) in multimode fibers introduces spatial degrees of freedom for ultrashort pulse generation, yet flexible manipulation of transverse mode compositions within multimode solitons remains challenging. Here, we propose a spectrum-to-mode mapping strategy in multimode Mamyshev oscillators (MOs) to selectively synchronize specific transverse modes through synergistic cross-phase modulation and offset spectral filtering. Meanwhile, four-wave mixing acts to stabilize intermodal phase relationships, facilitating selective STML characterized by diverse mode compositions with matched group velocities. Spatiotemporal solitons containing the pure LP01 mode, degenerate LP11 modes, or LP02+LP21 composite modes are selectively realized and mapped across the parameter space spanned by intracavity gain and filter detuning. Furthermore, intracavity collisions between coexisting mode groups with disparate group velocities are demonstrated to enable dynamic mode selection. Beyond the simulation of six modes in graded-index multimode fibers, selective STML is also demonstrated in MOs based on step-index multimode fibers and fibers supporting more transverse modes, confirming the generality of our approach. This strategy offers a versatile and robust pathway for transverse mode regulation and provides new insights into full dimensional structured light manipulation in multimode ultrafast fiber lasers.

title: Clifford Invariants and Three-Copy Quantum Tests
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14758v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We give an explicit treatment of the third tensor power of the Clifford representation on $n$ qutrits, for $n\geq2$. This representation has five pairwise inequivalent irreducible constituents, with multiplicities $1,1,1,1,2$. The decomposition reduces the Clifford twirl of a tensor cube to four real parameters. Two of them are spectral moments of the input. The other two are cubic invariants expressed as sums of cubes of the Weyl characteristic function and the discrete Wigner function. On trace-one Hermitian matrices, the invariant polynomials of degree at most three are spanned by the constant function and four algebraically independent functions. These functions do not separate Clifford orbits. For pure inputs a single parameter suffices. We recover its range and the characterization of its maximum by stabilizer states. We bound the stabilizer fidelity, determine full separability across the three copies in the symmetric family, and recover the criterion for a complex projective $3$-design. We classify the jointly invariant quantum Boolean functions. For stabilizer testing and for testing unknown observables we give explicit bounds on copies and queries. We also give character formulas for the finite projective Clifford groups and record the complete character table for two qutrits.

title: Avoiding Defects within Heavy-Hexagon Architecture
abstract:
arXiv:2610.14778v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When implementing scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing using superconducting quantum processors, one of the critical challenges to overcome is the presence of defective qubits arising from fabrication and calibration imperfections. A defect on a specific qubit severely restricts the connectivity between adjacent qubits, disrupts stabilizer measurements, induces frequent detection events, and consequently inflates the logical error rate. To mitigate this issue, various strategies have been proposed, such as syndrome extraction circuits based on stabilizer folding and the construction of super-stabilizers via gauge operators. However, these methods have primarily been developed for architectures with relatively high connectivity of 3 to 4. Furthermore, experimental demonstrations showing an actual reduction in logical error rates in the presence of physical hardware defects have been lacking. In this work, we propose a defect-avoidance scheme tailored for the heavy-hexagon architecture, which features a lower connectivity of 2 to 3. While previous approaches required four measurement cycles to measure all gauge operators comprising a super-stabilizer, our proposed scheme completes all gauge measurements within only two cycles. We experimentally validate this approach on IBM quantum hardware by identifying physical defects and implementing the defect-avoidance circuits. As a result, avoiding the defect yields an approximately 10\% reduction in the logical error rate per cycle for both logical $X$ and $Z$ errors. These findings demonstrate that defects in superconducting hardware can be successfully handled even under the constrained connectivity of heavy-hexagon lattices, and that defect avoidance substantially reduces logical errors on real quantum hardware.
